lede: You already enlarge shapes by 3, or by a half: every point moves further from, or closer to, a centre. A negative scale factor adds one thing. The image crosses to the other side of the centre and comes out upside down, the way a pinhole camera turns a picture over.
can: Enlarge a point or a shape by counting from the centre and reversing the steps.
Describe an enlargement fully: the word, the factor with its sign, the centre.
Scale lengths by the size of the factor and areas by its square.

caption: Scale factor −2 about C (−1, 1): each image corner is twice as far from C, on the other side, and T′ is upside down.

text: The other side of the centre

md: In the drawing, every dashed line runs from a corner of T, through C, and out the other side to the matching corner of T′. Each image corner is twice as far from C as its partner, but on the opposite side: that is what scale factor $-2$ means.

title: Why count from the centre
md: Multiplying the coordinates themselves by $-2$ only works when the centre is the origin, because then the steps from the centre are the coordinates. Anywhere else, count the steps from C, multiply those, and count back out from C.

stem: Enlarge the corner $(3, 2)$ of triangle T by scale factor $-2$ about C$(-1, 1)$.

steps.working: From C$(-1, 1)$ to $(3, 2)$: 4 right and 1 up
steps.decision: Count the steps from the centre, never from the origin.

steps.working: Times $-2$: 8 left and 2 down
steps.decision: The size 2 doubles each step; the minus sign turns right into left and up into down.

steps.working: Count that out from C: $(-9, -1)$
steps.decision: The image corner lands on the far side of C, twice as far away.

prompt: The point $(3, 4)$ is enlarged by scale factor $-2$ with centre $(0, 2)$. Where is its image?
explain: Count from the centre, as in step 1 of See it: (3, 4) is 3 right and 2 up of (0, 2). Times −2 gives 6 left and 4 down, which lands on (−6, −2).

twin.prompt: The point $(5, 1)$ is enlarged by scale factor $-2$ with centre $(2, -2)$. Where is its image?
twin.explain: (5, 1) is 3 right and 3 up of the centre; times −2 that is 6 left and 6 down, so the image is (−4, −8).

optionNotes.why: The minus sign has been dropped, so the image stays on the same side of the centre.
These are the coordinates times −2, which skips the centre altogether.
Same distance, other side: that is −1, and the factor here doubles the distance.
Doubling the steps is right, but keeping them the same way round forgets the minus sign, which sends the image across the centre.
Multiplying the coordinates only works when the centre is the origin; here the steps must be counted from the centre.
This crosses the centre but stays the same distance away, which is scale factor −1, not −2.

text: The whole shape, one corner at a time

md: A shape is its corners. Enlarge each corner on its own, counting from the centre every time, and join them only when all are marked. The image is the same shape turned upside down, with every length multiplied by the size of the factor.

title: November 2025, M8 Paper 1 Q12
md: A triangle enlarged by $-3$ about a centre off the origin. Just over half had every mark, and about one in ten had only one corner of the image right. Every corner needs its own count.

stem: Enlarge triangle T, with corners $(1, 2)$, $(3, 2)$ and $(1, 3)$, by scale factor $-2$ about C$(-1, 1)$.

steps.working: $(1, 2)$ is 2 right and 1 up of C, so its image is 4 left and 2 down: $(-5, -1)$
steps.decision: Corner by corner, each counted from C.

steps.working: $(3, 2)$ is 4 right and 1 up of C, so 8 left and 2 down: $(-9, -1)$
steps.decision: The corner from the first See it, the same count.

steps.working: $(1, 3)$ is 2 right and 2 up of C, so 4 left and 4 down: $(-5, -3)$
steps.decision: The last corner gets its own count too; copying the shape across from the first corner would keep the old size.
Join only now. Check: the image is on the far side of C, upside down, and twice as long in every direction.

title: Enlargements with Negative Scale Factors - Corbettmaths
why: Corbettmaths video 108 draws the lines through the centre and steps back along them, corner by corner. Watch it beside the steps above, then answer the check.

prompt: A triangle with corners $(0, 2), (2, 2), (0, 3)$ is enlarged by scale factor $-2$ about $(-1, 0)$. Which are the corners of the image?
explain: Each corner gets its own count from the centre, as in steps 1 to 3 of See it: 3 right and 2 up becomes 6 left and 4 down, giving (−7, −4), and the same for the other two.

twin.prompt: A triangle with corners $(2, 3), (3, 3), (2, 5)$ is enlarged by scale factor $-2$ about $(-1, 2)$. Which are the corners of the image?
twin.explain: Count each corner from (−1, 2) and multiply by −2: the image corners are (−7, 0), (−9, 0), (−7, −4).

optionNotes.why: One corner was enlarged and the triangle copied round it, so the image keeps the old size.
The minus sign is missing, so the image is on the same side of the centre.
Multiplying the coordinates ignores the centre.
The first corner is right, but the rest were copied across at the old size instead of being counted from the centre.
These are twice as far on the same side, as if the factor were +2.
These are the corners' coordinates times −2, which only works when the centre is the origin.

caption: Scale factor −1/2: half as far from C, on the other side, so the image is smaller and upside down.

md: A factor between $-1$ and $0$ does two things at once. Its size, $\tfrac{1}{2}$, halves every distance from the centre, so the image is smaller. Its sign sends the image across the centre, upside down. The counting is the same: halve the steps and reverse them.

stem: Enlarge the triangle with corners $(3, 3)$, $(7, 3)$ and $(3, 5)$ by scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ about C$(-1, 1)$.

steps.working: $(3, 3)$ is 4 right and 2 up of C; half of that, reversed, is 2 left and 1 down: $(-3, 0)$
steps.decision: Halve each step and turn it round.

steps.working: $(7, 3)$ is 8 right and 2 up, so 4 left and 1 down: $(-5, 0)$
steps.decision: Every corner counted from C, as before.

steps.working: $(3, 5)$ is 4 right and 4 up, so 2 left and 2 down: $(-3, -1)$
steps.decision: The last corner; now join the three.

steps.working: Check: the base was 4 across, the image base is 2 across
steps.decision: Half as long and on the other side of C: that is what the factor promised.

prompt: The point $(5, 5)$ is enlarged by scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ with centre $(1, 3)$. Where is its image?
explain: Halve the steps from the centre and reverse them, as in step 1 of See it: (5, 5) is 4 right and 2 up of (1, 3), so the image is 2 left and 1 down of it: (−1, 2).

twin.prompt: The point $(0, 6)$ is enlarged by scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ with centre $(-4, 2)$. Where is its image?
twin.explain: (0, 6) is 4 right and 4 up of the centre; halved and reversed that is 2 left and 2 down, so (−6, 0).

optionNotes.why: The steps were halved but not reversed, so the minus sign was lost.
These are the coordinates halved and negated, without the centre.
That is scale factor −2, the reciprocal of the one asked for.
Halving the steps is right, but not reversing them leaves the image on the same side of the centre.
Halving the coordinates themselves skips the centre, and lands off the grid points here.
Doubling instead of halving uses the factor upside down: −2 makes the image bigger.

caption: A and its image B. The centre is where the lines joining matching corners cross.

md: A full description earns one mark for each of three things: the word enlargement, the scale factor with its sign, and the centre as a coordinate pair. Leave one out and that mark goes.

Find the centre by joining two corners to their partners: the lines cross at it. The size of the factor is the image's distance from the centre over the object's; the sign is minus when the image is on the far side.

stem: Triangle A has corners $(5, 3), (9, 3), (5, 5)$ and triangle B has corners $(2, -3), (0, -3), (2, -4)$. Describe fully the transformation that takes A to B.

steps.decision: Matching corners joined; where the lines cross is the centre.

steps.working: From $(3, -1)$: $(5, 3)$ is 2 right and 4 up; $(2, -3)$ is 1 left and 2 down
steps.decision: Compare the steps to a corner with the steps to its image.

steps.working: Half as far, on the other side: scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$
steps.decision: Size: 1 step for every 2. Sign: minus, because B is across the centre from A.

steps.working: Enlargement, scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, centre $(3, -1)$
steps.decision: All three parts on the answer line: the word earns its own mark.

prompt: One enlargement maps $(4, 6)$ to $(-5, 0)$ and $(6, 6)$ to $(-6, 0)$. Which is its full description?
explain: Check a corner, as in steps 2 and 3 of See it: from (−2, 2), (4, 6) is 6 right and 4 up and (−5, 0) is 3 left and 2 down, half as far on the other side. A full description names the word, the factor with its sign and the centre.

twin.prompt: One enlargement maps $(7, 1)$ to $(1, 4)$ and $(9, 1)$ to $(0, 4)$. Which is its full description?
twin.explain: From (3, 3), (7, 1) is 4 right and 2 down and its image is 2 left and 1 up: half as far, across the centre, so −1/2 about (3, 3).

optionNotes.why: Without the centre, one of the three marks is lost.
The image is across the centre, so the factor needs its minus sign.
−2 would make the image twice as far away; it is half as far.
The word and the factor are right, but the centre carries its own mark and it is missing.
Leaving off the minus sign describes an image on the same side of the centre.
The image is half as far away, so the factor is −1/2; −2 is its reciprocal.

text: Lengths and areas: the sign drops out

md: Distances from the centre are multiplied by the size of the factor, so every length in the shape is too: scale factor $-3$ makes each side 3 times as long. Areas multiply by the square of the factor, and squaring removes the minus, so no length or area is ever negative.

title: Why −1 is a half turn
md: Scale factor $-1$ keeps every distance from the centre and sends each point straight across it. That is exactly a rotation of $180^{\circ}$ about the centre: the same size, upside down.

stem: A shape has perimeter $14$ cm and area $12\ \text{cm}^2$. It is enlarged by scale factor $-1.5$. Find the perimeter and the area of the image.

steps.working: Length factor: the size of $-1.5$, which is $1.5$
steps.decision: Lengths use the size; the sign only says which side of the centre.

steps.working: Perimeter $= 14 \times 1.5 = 21$ cm
steps.decision: Every side is stretched by the same factor, so the perimeter is too.
Square the factor, sign and all: the square is positive.

steps.working: Area $= 12 \times 2.25 = 27\ \text{cm}^2$
steps.decision: An area is never negative, whatever the sign of the factor.

prompt: A shape of area $45\ \text{cm}^2$ is enlarged by scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{3}$. What is the area of the image?
explain: Areas multiply by the square of the factor, as in step 3 of See it: (−1/3)² = 1/9, so 45 × 1/9 = 5 cm². The square is positive, so the area is too.

twin.prompt: A shape of area $36\ \text{cm}^2$ is enlarged by scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$. What is the area of the image?
twin.explain: The area factor is (−1/2)² = 1/4, so 36 × 1/4 = 9 cm², positive.

optionNotes.why: Squaring −1/2 gives +1/4, so the area stays positive.
Halving is the length factor; areas use its square, a quarter.
Multiplying by 4 makes the image bigger, but a factor of size 1/2 shrinks it.
The minus belongs to the factor, not the area: squaring removes it, so an area is never negative.
Multiplying by 1/3 uses the length factor; areas need its square, 1/9.
Multiplying by 9 turns the factor upside down; the image is smaller, so its area is too.

md: **A printed grid, a centre off the origin.** The usual 3-mark question (Summer 2023 Paper 1 Q7, November 2025 Paper 1 Q12). Marks come corner by corner, and correct work from a clearly marked wrong centre still earns one.
**A negative fraction.** Scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ has been drawn (November 2024 Paper 1 Q10) and described (Summer 2019 Paper 2 Q10, Summer 2025 Paper 2 Q9). Halve the steps and reverse them.
**Two in a row.** A reflection, then an enlargement (Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q6, Summer 2025 Paper 2 Q8): enlarge the first image, not the original, and draw both.

stem: Reflect the triangle with corners $(1, 2), (1, 4), (2, 2)$ in the line $y = x$, then enlarge that image by scale factor $-2$ about $(0, 1)$.

steps.working: Reflect in $y = x$: swap each pair, giving $(2, 1), (4, 1), (2, 2)$
steps.decision: The line y = x swaps the two coordinates of every corner.

steps.working: Enlarge that image: $(2, 1)$ is 2 right of $(0, 1)$, so $(-4, 1)$
steps.decision: The second transformation acts on the first image, never on the original.

steps.working: The other two: $(-8, 1)$ and $(-4, -1)$
steps.decision: Each corner counted from the centre, as always.

prompt: Reflect the point $(4, 1)$ in $y = x$, then enlarge its image by scale factor $-2$ about $(0, 2)$. Where does it end up?
explain: Reflect first, as in step 1 of See it: (4, 1) becomes (1, 4). Then count from the centre: 1 right and 2 up, times −2 is 2 left and 4 down, so (−2, −2).

twin.prompt: Reflect the point $(5, 2)$ in $y = x$, then enlarge its image by scale factor $-1$ about $(1, 2)$. Where does it end up?
twin.explain: (5, 2) reflects to (2, 5); that is 1 right and 3 up of the centre, and scale factor −1 reverses it: (0, −1).

optionNotes.why: The half turn was done before the reflection, which is the wrong order here.
The reflection was skipped, so the half turn acted on the original point.
This is only the reflected point; the enlargement still has to act on it.
This enlarges the original point and reflects afterwards, the transformations in the wrong order.
This enlarges the original point and never reflects it.
The reflection is right, but doubling without reversing drops the minus sign.

text: Going further: back to the centre

md: Harder questions give a corner and its image and ask for the centre, or ask for the enlargement that undoes one. The centre lies on the line joining a corner to its image, splitting it in the ratio of the distances. The undoing factor is the reciprocal, sign kept.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Matrices for enlargements, invariant points and centres that are not whole-number points are beyond this specification.

stem: Under an enlargement of scale factor $-2$, the point $(1, 3)$ maps to $(-5, 0)$. Find the centre, and the factor that maps $(-5, 0)$ back to $(1, 3)$.

steps.working: From $(1, 3)$ to $(-5, 0)$ is 6 left and 3 down
steps.decision: The centre is on this line, between the two points because the factor is negative.

steps.working: The distances are in the ratio $1 : 2$, so the centre is a third of the way along from the object point
steps.decision: The image is twice as far from the centre as the object, so the join splits 1 to 2.

steps.working: A third of that is 2 left and 1 down: centre $(-1, 2)$
steps.decision: Check: from the centre, (1, 3) is 2 right and 1 up and (−5, 0) is 4 left and 2 down.

steps.working: Back again: scale factor $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ about $(-1, 2)$
steps.decision: Undoing multiplies by 1 over −2: the reciprocal, still negative, the same centre.

prompt: Under an enlargement of scale factor $-2$, the point $(5, 2)$ maps to $(-4, -7)$. Where is the centre?
explain: The centre splits the join in the ratio 1 : 2, a third of the way from the object point, as in steps 2 and 3 of See it: (5, 2) to (−4, −7) is 9 left and 9 down, a third of which is 3 left and 3 down, giving (2, −1).

twin.prompt: Under an enlargement of scale factor $-2$, the point $(4, 5)$ maps to $(-5, -4)$. Where is the centre?
twin.explain: A third of the way from (4, 5) towards (−5, −4) is (1, 2): from there the image is twice as far, on the other side.

optionNotes.why: Halfway only fits scale factor −1; −2 splits the join 1 to 2.
The centre is nearer the object point, not the image.
A positive factor would put the centre outside the join.
The midpoint would be right for scale factor −1, but here the image is twice as far from the centre, so the split is 1 to 2.
A third of the way from the image end puts the centre nearer the image, but the object point is the nearer one.
This treats the factor as +2, which puts the centre outside the join instead of between the points.

md:
Count the steps from the centre to each corner and multiply them by the factor, sign and all.
Enlarge every corner on its own and join up last; a fraction shrinks as well as crossing.
Describe fully: enlargement, the factor with its sign, the centre as a coordinate pair.
Scale lengths by the size of the factor and areas by its square; neither is ever negative.

Expect an enlargement question most series, 2 to 4 marks: draw the image for a negative or fractional factor about a centre off the origin, or describe a given enlargement fully. Drawing marks go corner by corner, so write each image corner down as you find it; describing marks go one each to the word, the signed factor and the centre. Stuck: enlarge one corner by counting from the centre.
